ideas.title: Keyhold
ideas.novelty: Ownership of a placed tile is expressed purely by which physical tooth-key family its tab/notch edges belong to (a single wide tooth vs. a pair of narrow teeth), so tiles only mechanically interlock with same-owner neighbors and merely abut opposing ones -- no prior product encodes territorial ownership as a proprietary interlocking key profile. Search run: 'board game interlocking tiles proprietary tab notch key ownership physical fit no color' turned up laser-cut tile generators and generic interlocking-tile patents, none of which tie the tooth profile itself to player ownership as a game mechanic.
ideas.concept: Two players fill a fixed 7x7 grid of raised platforms with square keyed tiles, one per turn, trying to grow the longest unbroken chain of their own tiles that are all physically interlocked tab-into-notch. Every tile edge is either a tab or a notch, and every tile belongs to one of two tooth families -- a single wide tooth or a pair of narrow teeth -- so a tab only truly seats into a notch of its own family; edges that meet the wrong family, or an empty gap, simply sit flush without locking. A turn is just 'place a tile, choose its rotation to try to lock onto your own chain.' At game end both players trace their longest all-locked chain by feel and count; longest chain wins.

art_direction.form_language: Blocky, puzzle-piece geometry throughout -- thick square tiles with chunky mating teeth, no thin webs or filigree, everything reads as machined key-stock.
art_direction.silhouette: A flat square board bristling with a tidy 7x7 array of raised square pedestals, each topped by a slightly overhanging keyed tile so the whole thing reads as a shallow waffle grid from across the table.
art_direction.part_vocabulary: Board (one flat slab with 49 square pedestal bosses, immovable); Family-A tile (square block, tab/notch edges cut with one 10mm-wide central tooth); Family-B tile (square block, tab/notch edges cut with two 4mm teeth separated by a 2mm gap) -- the two tile families are told apart purely by tooth count, never by size or color.
art_direction.surface_treatment: Tabs protrude 4mm proud of the tile edge face; notches are cut 4mm deep into the edge face at matching width; no decorative engraving beyond the functional teeth.
art_direction.scale: Board footprint 220x220x10mm; each pedestal boss 24x24mm standing 3mm proud with 4mm gaps between bosses; each tile 22x22x8mm, handled easily between two fingers.
art_direction.hero_shot: Overhead product shot of the fully filled 7x7 grid mid-game, showing two visibly distinct tooth patterns snapped together into interlocking runs across the board, with a few tiles lifted just off their pedestals to show the tab/notch profiles in the air.

ideas.rules: Players: 2. Setup: place the board on the table; each player takes 20 identical-family tiles (Player Single takes 20 single-wide-tooth tiles, Player Twin takes 20 double-narrow-tooth tiles). The 7x7 grid has 49 empty pedestals. Turn structure: starting with Player Single, players alternate placing exactly one tile from their hand onto any empty pedestal, choosing the tile's rotation (0/90/180/270 degrees). Whenever a placed tile's edge lies flush against an already-placed tile of the SAME family, and one edge shows a tab and the other shows a matching notch, that seam is considered locked (physically, the tab is seated in the notch). Edges that meet an opposing-family tile, an empty pedestal, or a tab-against-tab/notch-against-notch pairing remain unlocked but the tiles may still occupy adjacent pedestals with no penalty. Play continues until both players have placed all 20 tiles (40 tiles total on the 49-pedestal board, 9 pedestals remain empty). Scoring: each player identifies their own single longest chain of tiles that are ALL mutually locked in one unbroken connected group (a tile counts toward the chain only if every connection to its chain neighbors is a true locked tab/notch seam). The player with the longer chain wins; ties are broken by the count of the second-longest chain, then by total number of locked seams overall.
ideas.components: 1 board slab, 220x220x10mm, with a fixed 7x7 array of 49 square pedestal bosses (24x24mm, 3mm proud, 4mm gaps), permanently part of the board. 20 Family-Single tiles, 22x22x8mm, each edge cut with either a single 10mm-wide, 4mm-proud tab or a matching 4mm-deep notch. 20 Family-Twin tiles, 22x22x8mm, each edge cut with either a pair of 4mm-wide, 4mm-proud tabs (2mm gap between them) or the matching pair of notches. No cards, no rulebook, no color.

must_survive.feature: All 40 tiles are separate loose bodies distinct from the board and from each other, not fused into the pedestal grid.
must_survive.visual: ortho_TOP_+Z: 40 discrete square tiles visibly resting on separate pedestals with a visible gap or seam line at every edge, not a continuous printed grid.

must_survive.feature: The board carries exactly 49 raised square pedestal bosses arranged in a 7x7 grid, each a distinct stepped-up platform.
must_survive.visual: ortho_TOP_+Z: a 7x7 array of 49 square bosses, each with a visible stepped edge separating it from the base slab and from its neighbors.

must_survive.feature: Family-Single tiles show one wide tooth per keyed edge while Family-Twin tiles show two narrow teeth per keyed edge, so the two ownership families are distinguishable by tooth count alone.
must_survive.visual: iso_front close-up on one tile of each family: one shows a single centered tooth per edge, the other shows two smaller teeth with a visible gap between them.

must_survive.feature: At least one seam between two same-family tiles shows the tab fully seated inside the matching notch, in contact, without collision or a visible gap.
must_survive.visual: iso_front on one locked seam: the tab of one tile visibly disappears into the notch of its neighbor with no daylight showing between them.

must_survive.feature: The tile set splits evenly into 20 Family-Single and 20 Family-Twin bodies, with no tile ambiguous between the two tooth profiles.
must_survive.visual: ortho_TOP_+Z: scanning the full board, every placed tile's edges clearly match one of exactly two tooth patterns, never a mix or a blank edge.

ideas.prompt: A flat square tabletop game board, roughly 220mm across, its top face covered in a tidy 7x7 grid of raised square platforms with visible gaps between them. Sitting on most of the platforms are two families of thick square puzzle-key tiles: one family shows a single wide protruding tooth on each edge, the other shows a pair of narrower protruding teeth on each edge, with matching notch cutouts on their opposite edges. Several tiles are interlocked into a snaking connected chain across the board where the teeth visibly seat into the notches of touching tiles; a few tiles sit unconnected on empty platforms, and a couple of loose tiles are shown lifted just above the board to reveal their tab-and-notch edge profile. Photographed as an unpainted single-material product shot, natural studio lighting, sharp focus on the tooth geometry.

ideas.title: Twin Deck Solitaire
ideas.novelty: Base game: classic English 33-hole cross-shaped peg solitaire. Genuine rule-level change: two identical boards are stacked with a fixed air gap and hole-for-hole vertical alignment, a new 'transfer' move lets a peg drop straight between the aligned hole on the other layer as an entire turn (no capture), and the game is converted from a single-player 'reduce to one peg' puzzle into a 2-player adversarial contest where the player who runs out of legal moves loses. Search run: 'two-layer 3D peg solitaire board game vertical jumps between stacked boards' returned only theoretical/mathematical treatments of 3D solitaire position classes and no shipped product with a stacked-board transfer-move mechanic.
ideas.concept: Classic peg solitaire's cross-shaped board is doubled: two identical hole grids sit stacked on posts with a real air gap between them, every hole vertically aligned with its twin below or above. Players alternate turns, and instead of only jumping pegs within one layer, a player may spend a turn 'dropping' a peg straight down (or up) into its empty twin hole on the other layer, opening up jump lines that were previously blocked. Whoever leaves their opponent with no legal jump or transfer loses; reducing the whole rig to a single peg is an instant win either way.

art_direction.form_language: Two thick cross-shaped plates held apart on stout cylindrical posts, reading as a compact two-story rig; pegs are plain stubby cylinders, nothing tapered or filigreed.
art_direction.silhouette: From the side, two parallel cross-shaped decks with visible daylight between them, connected only at the four corners by posts, like a small equipment rack.
art_direction.part_vocabulary: Top board and bottom board (identical 33-hole cross plates); 4 corner support posts (plain cylinders); 64 pegs (identical plain cylinders) -- the only shape families in the whole game, distinguished from each other purely by which body they are, not by any per-player marking since the game has no owned pieces.
art_direction.surface_treatment: 33 through- or blind-holes per board, 12mm diameter, arranged in the standard peg-solitaire cross; no other surface texture.
art_direction.scale: Each board 180x180x12mm; 30mm vertical gap between boards; posts 60mm tall x 10mm diameter; pegs 10mm diameter x 20mm tall, holes 12mm diameter x 8mm deep minimum.
art_direction.hero_shot: Three-quarter product shot of the full stacked rig mid-game, pegs filling most holes on both layers, one peg frozen mid-drop between a top hole and its empty aligned hole below, showing the transfer move in action.

ideas.rules: Players: 2. Setup: assemble the rig -- two identical 33-hole cross boards held 30mm apart by four corner posts, holes vertically aligned pair-for-pair. Fill every hole on both boards with a peg except the center hole of the top board and the center hole of the bottom board (32 pegs per layer, 64 total; 2 holes start empty, one per layer). Turn structure: players alternate turns; the current player must make exactly one of two legal move types if any exist: (a) Jump move -- within a single layer only, jump one peg orthogonally over an adjacent occupied hole into an empty hole two spaces beyond in a straight line, removing the jumped peg from the board entirely (identical to classic peg solitaire jumps); or (b) Transfer move -- choose a peg sitting in a hole on one layer whose vertically-aligned twin hole on the other layer is currently empty, and move that single peg straight through the gap into the aligned hole; no peg is removed on a transfer. Win conditions: if the total peg count on the whole rig is reduced to exactly 1 by a jump, the player who made that jump wins immediately. Otherwise, if a player has no legal jump on either layer and no legal transfer available at the start of their turn, that player loses immediately. Passing is not allowed if a legal move exists.
ideas.components: 2 identical cross-shaped boards, 180x180x12mm, each with 33 holes (12mm diameter, minimum 8mm deep) in the standard English peg-solitaire cross layout, holes on the two boards vertically aligned to each other. 4 corner support posts, 10mm diameter x 60mm tall, press-fit between the two boards to hold a fixed 30mm gap. 64 identical cylindrical pegs, 10mm diameter x 20mm tall. No cards, no rulebook, no color.

must_survive.feature: The two boards are held in a fixed parallel stack with a clear open air gap between them, not touching or fused into one solid block.
must_survive.visual: iso_front: two distinct flat boards visibly separated by open space, connected only by four slender posts at the corners, daylight clearly visible between the plates.

must_survive.feature: Each board carries 33 genuinely pierced or drilled holes in the standard cross layout (66 total), not shallow decorative dimples.
must_survive.visual: ortho_TOP_+Z on each board: 33 clearly visible circular holes arranged in the classic peg-solitaire cross pattern.

must_survive.feature: 64 pegs exist as separate loose cylindrical bodies, not fused to a board or to each other.
must_survive.visual: iso_front: 64 individually distinguishable cylindrical pegs visibly seated in holes, each one appearing liftable and separate from the board body.

must_survive.feature: Every one of the 33 hole positions on the top board sits in true vertical alignment with its twin hole on the bottom board, forming a real straight-through transfer channel.
must_survive.visual: ortho_FRONT: a peg dropped through one transfer channel lines up with no visible lateral offset between its top-board and bottom-board holes.

must_survive.feature: Each peg is a snug, removable friction fit in the 12mm holes -- close enough to stay seated, loose enough to lift out by hand.
must_survive.visual: iso_front: pegs sit flush and level across both boards at a consistent height, none tilted or proud, none jammed.

ideas.prompt: A compact two-story tabletop game rig: two identical thick cross-shaped plates, each about 180mm across and pierced with 33 round holes in the classic peg-solitaire cross pattern, held one above the other on four short cylindrical posts with a clear open air gap of about 30mm between the plates. Most holes on both plates are filled with plain stubby cylindrical pegs standing upright, a few holes left empty, and one peg is shown frozen mid-drop in the open gap directly between a hole on the top plate and its empty aligned hole on the bottom plate, illustrating a vertical transfer move. Photographed as an unpainted single-material product shot, clean studio lighting, camera angle low enough to show the gap between the two decks clearly.

ideas.title: Eclipse
ideas.novelty: Reskin of Othello/Reversi with zero rule change: the two 'colors' Othello normally needs are replaced by a single reversible disc shape whose two faces are geometrically opposite -- one a raised dome, one a sunken dish -- so flipping a disc during a capture is a literal physical inversion of relief rather than a color swap, which is the most literal geometry-only translation of Othello's flip mechanic possible. Search run: 'Othello Reversi tactile edition discs convex dome vs flat instead of color' returned only standard black/white retail editions and generic tactile-accessibility discussions, no shipped product using a dome/dish relief pair as the flip mechanic.
ideas.concept: Eclipse is Othello/Reversi played exactly by the book, restyled so ownership lives in relief instead of color: every disc has a domed 'sun' face and a dished 'crater' face, and flipping a disc during a flanking capture physically inverts which relief faces up. One turn is a placement that sandwiches a straight line of opposing-face discs between the new disc and another same-face disc, flipping the whole line's relief.

art_direction.form_language: A single flat plate perforated with a grid of shallow round sockets, filled with thick lens-shaped discs whose two faces bulge and dish in mirror image -- smooth, continuous curvature, no sharp ornamentation.
art_direction.silhouette: From across the table it reads as a checkerboard grid of small bumps and craters rather than a flat mosaic, the relief itself doing the work color normally does.
art_direction.part_vocabulary: Board (one flat slab with an 8x8 grid of 64 shallow circular sockets); disc (64 identical reversible pieces, one face a proud dome, the opposite face a recessed dish) -- only two shape families exist in the whole game, and the second is really one shape read two ways.
art_direction.surface_treatment: Dome face rises 4mm proud of the disc's flat rim; dish face sinks 4mm below the same rim; both are smooth continuous curves, no engraving.
art_direction.scale: Board footprint 220x220x12mm; sockets 24mm diameter, 5mm deep, 2mm gap between neighboring sockets; discs 24mm diameter x 8mm thick overall (rim to rim), each face's relief adding roughly 4mm beyond the flat rim.
art_direction.hero_shot: Overhead shot of a mid-game board with a mix of dome-up and dish-up discs scattered across the grid in a clear flanking pattern, one disc held above an empty socket about to be placed, lighting raking across the surface so the relief pattern is unmistakable even without any color.

ideas.rules: Players: 2 (Dome and Dish). Setup: place the board with its empty 8x8 socket grid. Seat 4 discs in the four center sockets in a diagonal pattern: two opposite corners of the center 2x2 block show dome face up, the other two opposite corners show dish face up. Dome moves first. Turn structure: on your turn you must place one disc from the shared supply into any empty socket, oriented with your face up (Dome player places dome-face-up, Dish player places dish-face-up), such that the new disc flanks one or more straight unbroken lines (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal) of the opponent's face-up discs, with one of your own face-up discs anchoring the far end of each such line. Every opposing disc in each flanked line is then physically flipped over in place so it now shows your face up. If a player has no legal flanking placement, they must pass; if neither player can move, or the board fills, the game ends. Scoring: count discs showing dome face up versus dish face up across the whole board; whichever face has more discs showing wins the game. Ties are a draw.
ideas.components: 1 board slab, 220x220x12mm, with a fixed 8x8 grid of 64 shallow circular sockets (24mm diameter, 5mm deep, 2mm gaps). 64 identical reversible discs, 24mm diameter, roughly 8mm total thickness at the rim, one face a smooth dome rising 4mm proud of the rim, the opposite face a smooth dish sinking 4mm below the rim. No cards, no rulebook, no color.

must_survive.feature: All 64 discs are separate loose bodies, distinct from the board and each other, not fused into the socket grid.
must_survive.visual: ortho_TOP_+Z: 64 discrete circular discs visibly resting in sockets, each appearing individually liftable, not printed as a continuous surface.

must_survive.feature: Each disc has one face carrying a dome that protrudes above its flat rim and the opposite face carrying a dish recessed below that same rim, so the two faces are unmistakably different in relief.
must_survive.visual: iso_front close-up on a single disc shown from both sides: one face clearly bulges outward into a dome, the other clearly sinks inward into a dish.

must_survive.feature: The board carries exactly 64 shallow circular sockets arranged in an 8x8 grid, each sized to seat one disc.
must_survive.visual: ortho_TOP_+Z: an unmistakable 8x8 grid of 64 circular depressions across the board's top face.

must_survive.feature: A disc seated in its socket, whichever face is up, does not collide with the board or with discs in neighboring sockets, and can be lifted back out by hand.
must_survive.visual: iso_front: discs sit level in their sockets with a visible gap to every neighboring socket, no overlap or wedging between adjacent discs.

must_survive.feature: The board is a single flat square slab with the 8x8 socket grid centered and symmetric, reading clearly as a Reversi-style board despite carrying no color cues.
must_survive.visual: ortho_TOP_+Z: the socket grid is evenly spaced and centered on the board with equal margins on all four sides.

ideas.prompt: A flat square game board about 220mm across, its top face perforated with a clean 8x8 grid of shallow round sockets. Scattered across most of the sockets are thick reversible discs, roughly 24mm across -- about half showing a smooth raised dome face rising proud of the socket, the other half showing a smooth sunken dish face recessed into the socket, arranged in the mid-game flanking pattern of a Reversi match. One extra disc is held just above an empty socket, tilted to show both its domed and dished faces at once. Photographed as an unpainted single-material product shot, raking studio light that makes the dome and dish relief pattern read clearly across the grid without any color.
